title: Palladium-hydride reservoir re-passivates traps during monthly healing sleep
idea: Time/scale jump (atomic bond -> years): a thin PdHx film inside the package releases H2 when the stack is warmed to ~150 C during a scheduled monthly 'healing sleep', re-passivating Si/SiO2 dangling bonds created by hot-carrier and hammer stress. Years of trap-generation aging are undone in hours instead of being covered by guard-banded refresh.
why: Retention tail and row-hammer drift grow with age; resetting interface trap density could hold end-of-life retention at time-zero values, letting fabs ship cells with ~2x less retention margin.

title: Fleet-wide weak-cell atlas predicts new dies' failures from lot genealogy
idea: Scale jump (one cell -> global fleet): aggregate ECC-corrected-error addresses from millions of deployed DIMMs, keyed by fab lot, wafer XY and die coordinate, into a Bayesian prior; a new die's likely weak rows are predicted from its genealogy and pre-mapped before boot. In-field profiling drops from hours to seconds and the prior catches rare tails that factory tests miss.
why: Retention/VRT tail coverage without long factory bakes; targets a ~5-10x reduction in uncorrected-error escapes and in test time per die.

title: Z-channel codes exploit leakage's one-way arrow of time
idea: Time-direction shift: true-cells only decay 1->0 and anti-cells only 0->1, so the error channel is asymmetric. Encode with asymmetric (Z-channel/Berger-style constant-weight) codes, matched to the true/anti layout, that spend parity only on the one possible flip direction.
why: Corrects about 2x more retention errors per parity bit than symmetric SECDED/BCH, permitting ~30% lower Cs or a longer refresh interval at equal reliability.

title: Rack-scale erasure-coded CXL pool accepts dies with dead banks
idea: Scale jump (bank -> rack): stripe pooled CXL memory with a 14+2 erasure code across 16 memory devices on different sleds, with lazy reconstruction of any failed bank. Dies with whole dead banks or high raw BER, now scrapped, are sold into the pool because the failure domain becomes the rack, not the die.
why: Raises sellable die yield by an estimated 5-10 points and lets the parity overhead (~12.5%) replace per-die repair area.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM routes around defects via on-wafer mesh
idea: Scale jump (die -> wafer): keep the 300 mm wafer whole, stitch reticles with a fault-tolerant mesh NoC, and at bring-up disable defective reticle tiles in software. Dicing, packaging and per-die yield loss disappear, so a die-killing defect costs one tile.
why: Usable-bit yield approaches ~95% vs ~80-85% die yield; also removes package/TSV cost and gives ~TB/s internal bandwidth.

title: Sell capacity-years: DIMMs that shrink gracefully as rows retire
idea: Time shift (time-zero spec -> lifetime contract): ship modules with weaker cells that the OS retires row by row as they degrade, and price them per guaranteed GB-year with a declining capacity curve (e.g. 100% -> 92% over 5 years). Today those weaker cells are screened out at the factory.
why: Lets fabs sell lower retention bins (an estimated 5-15% more good bits per wafer) and moves reliability from screening to contract.

title: Time-to-digital bitline sensing yields per-bit confidence for soft ECC
idea: Timescale shift (voltage amplitude -> picosecond timing): measure how many picoseconds the bitline takes to cross the sense threshold with a small TDC per sense-amp group. Slow crossings flag low-signal bits, and that soft information feeds an on-die soft-decision decoder.
why: Soft information roughly doubles correctable raw BER, letting Cs fall from ~5 fF toward ~3 fF or refresh slow ~2x (attacks the capacitor charge wall).

title: Row-buffer-wide long code computed over the full 8KB page
idea: Scale jump (64-bit word -> 8KB row): activation already latches the whole row into sense amps, so place a polar/LDPC code spanning the entire row and decode it in the row buffer during activation. The 128x overfetch becomes a reliability asset.
why: Parity overhead drops from 12.5% to ~3% while tolerating raw BER ~1e-4, enabling weaker or smaller cells and about 9% more capacity per die.

title: Silicon nanocrystal electron-sink layer between wordlines stops hammer migration
idea: Scale jump (single migrating electron -> system security): row hammer is partly driven by electrons injected from the aggressor's passing gate that diffuse to the victim storage node. Embed a deep-trap Si/Ge nanocrystal layer in the inter-wordline isolation to capture and recombine them before they arrive.
why: Could raise the hammer threshold from ~1k toward ~10k+ activations, removing most mitigation refresh and bandwidth tax.

title: Deliberately weakened honeypot rows give early hammer warning
idea: Scale jump (cell -> datacenter security): each bank includes canary rows with intentionally narrowed isolation that flip after ~200 activations of their known neighbors. The controller scrubs canaries every refresh window, and a flip tells it to migrate victims and alert fleet security long before real rows (~1k) fail.
why: Lets designers drop costly per-row activation counters (area ~1-2%) while still catching hammer patterns early.

title: Lifetime-typed allocation maps short-lived buffers to unrefreshed regions
idea: Timescale matching (data lifetime vs retention): the compiler/runtime tags each allocation with an expected lifetime (<1 ms, <64 ms, persistent) and the allocator places it in regions binned by retention. Short-lived buffers go to refresh-disabled or weak-cell regions that only have to hold data until it dies.
why: Cuts refresh energy (~16-33% of idle power) in AI workloads where most activations live under 10 ms, and gives weak-retention bins a use.

title: KV-cache precision decays with token age in leaky cells
idea: Time shift (data age = allowed precision): store the LSBs of older KV-cache tokens in unrefreshed weak cells and their MSBs in refreshed cells, so old context loses precision over seconds the way attention already discounts it. New tokens get full refresh.
why: Removes refresh for ~40-60% of KV bits and allows lower-grade cells for long-context inference memory.

title: Exponential-decay bloom filter tracks hours-long VRT toggling
idea: Timescale shift (64 ms refresh -> hours-long trap dwell): variable-retention-time cells flip between leaky and good trap states with hours-scale dwell. The controller keeps a time-decaying counting bloom filter of rows that recently showed corrected errors and refreshes only those fast, letting entries fade as the dwell statistics expire.
why: Handles the VRT tail that static retention profiling misses, enabling relaxed baseline refresh (e.g. 256 ms) with near-zero escapes.

title: 77 K liquid-nitrogen memory racks permit 1 fF capacitors
idea: Scale+temperature jump (cell -> rack-level cryostat): at 77 K junction and GIDL leakage fall by orders of magnitude, so retention runs from hours to days. Size cells for ~1 fF (shallower, AR ~20:1 pillars) and operate whole LN2-cooled memory racks almost refresh-free.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall and the refresh tail together: capacitor etch depth drops ~3x and refresh energy almost vanishes; cooling overhead is amortized at rack scale.

title: Self-clearing capacitor electrodes isolate dielectric breakdown spots
idea: Scale borrow (metallized-film power capacitor -> nanoscale DRAM pillar): use an ultra-thin top electrode that locally vaporizes or oxidizes around a dielectric breakdown spot, so a defect becomes a detectable open cell instead of a leaking short that disturbs neighbors.
why: Lets fabs push high-k dielectrics thinner and higher-k (toward the k~70 target) despite weak spots, because failures turn into ECC-friendly erasures.

title: Elastic spare rows borrowed from user capacity on demand
idea: Time shift (fab-time redundancy -> lifetime redundancy): instead of fixed spare rows burned at the fab, all rows ship as user capacity, and the controller later converts address-remapped rows into spares through a firmware remap table as wear and weak cells appear.
why: Recovers the ~2-4% of array area spent on idle redundancy at time zero and spends it only when needed.

title: Two-timescale ECC: light inline code plus strong background scrub
idea: Time split (ns access path vs seconds scrub path): reads use only a cheap SEC code, while a scrubber walking memory every few seconds checks and repairs it against a heavy erasure parity computed over 1 MB regions. The strong code never slows the critical path.
why: Tolerates ~100x higher accumulating retention error rates at ~4% total overhead, enabling longer refresh intervals.

title: Training-cluster checkpoints replace ECC for bulk activations
idea: Scale jump (bit -> datacenter job): large training runs already checkpoint every few minutes, so activation and optimizer memory on non-ECC, denser, cheaper DRAM accepts silent-error risk. Cross-replica gradient checksums detect corruption and the job rolls back.
why: Recovers the ~12.5% ECC capacity and lets accelerators use lower-binned parts; converts reliability into a time-rollback budget.

title: Garbage-collector compaction doubles as hardware refresh
idea: Timescale coupling (ms GC cycles <-> 64 ms refresh): managed runtimes rewrite live objects during compaction, so the controller exposes a 'freshly written' bit per row and skips refresh on heap regions rewritten within their retention window. Dead regions are never refreshed at all.
why: Cuts refresh operations on managed-heap memory by an estimated 30-70%, with weak-retention rows parked in high-churn nursery spaces.

title: Wafer-position-aware ECC strength fused per die
idea: Scale jump (wafer map -> die config): edge and notch-region dies show worse retention tails, so at sort each die's ECC mode (SEC vs DEC vs chipkill-lite) is fused based on its wafer radius and measured margin. Strong dies ship more user capacity and weak dies ship more parity.
why: Turns marginal edge dies into sellable parts and reclaims ~3-6% capacity on center dies.

title: Reverse-bias healing pulses empty traps during idle periods
idea: Timescale shift (seconds of stress -> milliseconds of recovery): during idle self-refresh windows, drive negative wordline and reverse storage-node bias pulses that detrap charge accumulated at the access-transistor interface, like NBTI recovery in logic.
why: Shrinks the aged leakage tail and the hammer susceptibility that grows over years, possibly holding retention near the time-zero distribution.

title: Adaptive twin-cell fusion of weak row pairs as cells age
idea: Time shift (static 1T1C -> on-the-fly 2T2C): when a row pair shows weak retention, the controller reconfigures them into a differential twin-cell pair (true and complement stored), halving that pair's capacity but doubling signal and cancelling common-mode leakage.
why: Rescues the weakest ~0.1-1% of rows at 2x local cost instead of discarding the die; a graceful-degradation path for aging.

title: Dynamic guard rows flank hot aggressors by migrating neighbors
idea: Scale/time shift (fixed layout -> runtime layout): when a row's activation rate crosses a threshold within a refresh window, the controller migrates its two physical neighbors' data elsewhere so the hot row is temporarily flanked by empty guard rows; the rows are re-filled when it cools.
why: Neutralizes hammer for the hot set at near-zero refresh cost, tolerating thresholds below 1k without per-row victim refresh storms.

title: Word-granular remap CAM absorbs directed-self-assembly line defects
idea: No EUV: pattern ~12 nm pitch wordlines with block-copolymer directed self-assembly on DUV guide patterns, accepting the ~0.1-1/cm2 dislocation defects. Scale shift (molecular dislocation -> 64-bit word): each defect is mapped at sort and absorbed by a per-bank content-addressable remap of 64-bit words.
why: Reaches near-EUV pitch without EUV tools (saves ~5-7 EUV layers of capex), with defect tolerance at a ~0.5% periphery cost.

title: Nanoimprint template defects become one shared repair map
idea: No EUV: nanoimprint lithography copies identical template defects onto every die at the same coordinates. Time/scale shift (one template -> millions of dies over its life): characterize the template once and pre-fuse one universal repair map into every die it prints, adding to the map only when the template degrades.
why: Removes most per-die repair test time and lets cheap NIL replace EUV for critical array layers despite its higher defect rate.

title: Large DUV cells store two bits each under Gray-coded LDPC
idea: No EUV: a 38 nm DUV-patterned cell can hold ~2-3x the charge of a 12 nm cell, so use four charge levels per cell (MLC DRAM) with Gray mapping and a row-level LDPC to absorb the level-tail errors. The retention budget is rescaled to 16 ms for the level spacing.
why: Recovers ~2x bits per cell to offset the coarser DUV pitch; a density step without EUV capex.

title: SAQP pitch-walk classes get their own refresh and ECC
idea: No EUV: self-aligned quadruple patterning on DUV produces systematic alpha/beta/gamma line-width classes. Scale shift (litho systematics -> refresh scheduling): tag each row by its spacer class at design time and run separate refresh intervals and ECC strengths per class rather than guard-banding all rows to the worst class.
why: Recovers ~20-40% of refresh energy and lets multi-patterning replace EUV despite its CD variation.

title: Retention-signature die matching when assembling stacks
idea: No EUV: mature DUV dies have wider retention spread. Scale shift (die test data -> package assembly): sort known-good dies into retention-signature bins and stack only matched dies, so each stack runs at its own refresh rate instead of the worst die's in a random mix; outlier dies go to high-refresh SKUs.
why: Cuts stack refresh overhead ~2x and raises usable yield of wide-spread DUV dies.

title: Hammer-immune coarse-pitch DUV memory sold as secure tier
idea: No EUV: hammer thresholds rise steeply with wordline pitch, so 25-30 nm-class DUV DRAM has thresholds of ~50k+ activations. Scale/time shift (old node reframed as security feature): market it as a premium hammer-immune tier for multi-tenant clouds and confidential computing.
why: Gives new US DUV fabs a profitable segment where the reliability gain pays for the density loss.

title: Multi-beam e-beam writes per-die personalized repair wiring
idea: No EUV: after wafer sort, a multi-beam e-beam writer exposes one custom upper-metal layer per die that physically reroutes around defective subarrays and bitlines, instead of using fuse banks.
why: Removes fuse/redundancy periphery area (part of the ~49% periphery tax) and gives finer-grained repair than spare rows.

title: Area-selective molecular monolayer passivates gate-edge GIDL sites
idea: No EUV: on DUV-defined buried-wordline recesses, a self-assembled monolayer deposited only on exposed Si/oxide edges (area-selective ALD inhibitor chemistry) passivates the gate-edge trap sites that cause the GIDL leakage tail. Molecular-scale chemistry stands in for nanometer patterning.
why: Could pull the ≤13 fA tail down ~3-10x so larger, cheaper DUV cells meet longer retention and refresh less.

title: Leakage-twin RC oscillator clocks each bank's refresh
idea: No EUV: build a tiny relaxation oscillator whose timing capacitor leaks through a replica access transistor drawn on the same DUV process. Its period tracks process, temperature and aging leakage directly, and it clocks refresh for its bank.
why: Refresh tracks real leakage instead of the worst-case 64 ms spec, saving an estimated 30-60% of refresh energy on wide-variation DUV silicon.

title: Revive depreciated 2010s DUV DRAM lines with weak-die-accepting ECC
idea: No EUV: buy or restart fully depreciated 30-40 nm DUV DRAM fabs whose capital cost is already written off, and ship their output with stronger on-module ECC and runtime row retirement so higher defect and retention-fail rates still meet spec. Time shift: a decade-old asset meets 2026 demand.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of leading-edge wafer cost, so these bits could be ~40-50% cheaper per wafer despite lower density; also usable for U.S. capacity.

title: Compression-funded ECC spends freed bytes on stronger parity
idea: No EUV: when a 64B line compresses to 48B, the controller stores 16B of extra parity in the freed space, raising correction from 1 to ~8 symbols for that line. Weak DUV arrays get strong protection without fixed overhead.
why: Allows raw BER ~10-100x higher on mature-node arrays at no capacity cost for compressible data (often >50% of lines).

title: ECC compresses the yield-learning curve from years to months
idea: No EUV: a new DUV DRAM line normally needs 18-24 months of yield learning before it can ship. Time shift: ship from month 3 with heavy on-die ECC plus OS row retirement covering immature defect density, then relax ECC by firmware as the line matures.
why: Brings new fab revenue and supply forward by about a year, which matters more than density during a 4x price spike.

title: Interposer ECC chiplet serves array-only DUV memory dies
idea: No EUV: strip ECC, repair logic and most periphery from the DUV memory die and put them on one mature-node logic chiplet on a silicon interposer that serves 8 array dies. The chiplet can run long codes across all of them.
why: Shrinks the ~49% periphery share on each DUV array die and pools reliability logic across dies at package scale.

title: Slew-shaped wordline pulses cut hammer coupling
idea: No EUV: drive wordlines with controlled 2-5 ns ramps and an early-close discharge profile instead of sharp sub-ns edges, reducing capacitive coupling and hot-electron injection into victim nodes. Timescale shift: the change is in ps-to-ns edge physics, not geometry.
why: Could raise hammer thresholds ~2-5x at no lithography cost, at a small tRAS penalty.

title: First-week in-field self-profiling replaces factory retention bakes
idea: No EUV: skip the hours-long high-temperature retention test at the factory. Time/scale shift (factory hours -> field week): the module ships with conservative refresh, self-profiles each row's retention during its first week in a server, then relaxes refresh row by row.
why: Cuts test capex and floor time (a major cost for mature-node fabs) and finds VRT/temperature-specific tails in their real environment.

title: Deep-trench high-capacitance cells push retention to seconds
idea: No EUV: revive deep-trench capacitors etched into the substrate under DUV-defined, larger cells (~30 fF), so stored charge dwarfs leakage. Retention moves from ~64 ms to ~1 s and the leakage tail stops dictating refresh.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth fall ~15x; DUV density loss is offset by no refresh tax and by stacking more dies.

title: Imprinted nanowire crossbar addressed by stochastic decoders
idea: No EUV: imprint or spacer-pattern sub-20 nm nanowire crossbars of gain cells, and address them through a decoder formed by randomly doped wire segments. Scale shift (molecular randomness -> addressing scheme): each array's random address code is discovered at test and mapped by software, so defects and randomness become part of addressing rather than yield loss.
why: Very high density from cheap patterning without EUV overlay accuracy; tolerates ~10-20% defective wires.

title: Rotating per-epoch scramble keys break pattern-dependent failures
idea: No EUV: mature-node arrays show data-pattern-dependent retention and coupling failures. Time shift: re-scramble each row with a new key every few refresh epochs during scrubbing, so no worst-case pattern stays in place long enough to fail and errors become random and ECC-friendly.
why: Narrows the pattern-dependent tail ~2-3x, letting DUV cells with more coupling pass spec.

title: Year-two DIMM remanufacturing: re-profile, re-fuse, resell
idea: No EUV: take back modules at year two, re-test them with fleet telemetry, re-fuse repairs and retire weak ranks, then resell them with a refreshed warranty. Time shift: product life runs past 5 years and needs no new wafers.
why: Stretches existing bit supply by ~30-50% of lifetime output with zero fab capex during the shortage.

title: Harvested DDR4 into heavily coded CXL memory pools
idea: No EUV: put DDR4 from decommissioned servers behind CXL controllers that add chipkill-plus-erasure coding and per-row retirement, tolerating aged parts with higher error rates. Existing silicon becomes a second-life memory tier.
why: Adds already-made bits to supply with zero lithography; aged-part reliability is covered at the controller.

title: FD-SOI back-gate trims each subarray's leakage over its lifetime
idea: No EUV: build the access array on DUV FD-SOI and give each subarray its own back-gate bias rail. Firmware re-trims back-bias yearly as aging shifts thresholds, keeping each subarray's leakage tail centered.
why: Tightens the retention distribution ~3-5x over life, allowing longer refresh on coarse-node silicon.

title: Sacrificial-etch air gaps isolate adjacent wordlines from hammer
idea: No EUV: at DUV pitch, a sacrificial carbon or oxide fill between buried wordlines is removed through DUV-defined vents and sealed, leaving air gaps (k=1) that cut aggressor-victim capacitive and trap coupling.
why: Could raise the hammer threshold ~3x and lower wordline capacitance (and CV2 energy) ~20%.

title: Federal reliability-graded memory standard creates demand for DUV parts
idea: No EUV: a U.S. procurement standard defines 'graded memory' (module-level ECC plus row retirement plus telemetry) so federal and hyperscale buyers can buy DUV-made, weaker-cell DRAM at full qualification. Policy shifts demand toward non-EUV domestic supply.
why: Creates a guaranteed market that de-risks new U.S. DUV DRAM fabs (US share now ~1-2%).
